title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 320: The Vertical Frontier: Elevators & Cities
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 320 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Vertical Frontier: Elevators, Steel, and Urban Stratification

Paragraph 1. Before the 1850s, city buildings rarely had more than five or six floors. The reason was simple: climbing lots of stairs was too tiring for human knees. Because nobody wanted to walk up six flights every day, top-floor rooms were cheap and unpopular, rented by servants, poor students, and young artists. Rich families lived on the first and second floors, where they did not have to climb high.

Paragraph 2. Everything changed in May 1854 at a big show in New York. Inventor Elisha Graves Otis stood on a high lifting platform and told a worker to cut the main rope. The crowd gasped, but the platform dropped only a few inches before his automatic safety brake locked it safely in place. Soon after, new steel frames replaced heavy stone walls, and cities began building tall skyscrapers.

Paragraph 3. With safe elevators, city life flipped completely upside down. Top floors quickly became the most expensive luxury homes, called penthouses. High above dusty streets, bad smells, and noisy traffic, rich buyers enjoyed bright sunlight, clean air, and wide views. Lower floors became ordinary shops and offices.

Paragraph 4. Sociologist Dr. Ronald Kroll says elevators also separated social classes. In old low buildings, rich and poor neighbours met every day on stairs and sidewalks. In modern skyscrapers, fast private elevators carry rich residents straight from underground car parks to top-floor apartments, so they rarely meet ordinary people on the street.

groups.title: Questions 1–4
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

q1.text: Why did buildings rarely rise above six floors before the 1850s?
options: A. Builders had no stone to make tall walls.
B. City laws banned tall apartment blocks.
C. Climbing too many stairs was exhausting for people.

steps: Đoạn 1: Leo nhiều bậc thang quá mệt cho đầu gối con người.

q2.text: What did Elisha Otis do at the 1854 New York show?
options: A. He proved his safety brake could stop a falling platform.
B. He built the first glass skyscraper in one day.
C. He climbed six flights of stairs faster than a crowd.

steps: Đoạn 2: Ông cho cắt dây cáp để chứng minh phanh an toàn chặn được bục rơi.

q3.text: How did safe elevators change top-floor apartments?
options: A. They were turned into noisy shops.
B. They became expensive luxury homes with clean air.
C. They were reserved strictly for poor students.

steps: Đoạn 3: Tầng trên cùng biến thành penthouse xa hoa, không khí sạch và view rộng.

q4.text: What social problem does Dr. Kroll blame on fast skyscraper elevators?
options: A. Rich people have less daily contact with ordinary citizens.
B. Underground car parks are too small for modern cars.
C. Elevators break down too often during rush hour.

steps: Đoạn 4: Thang máy riêng đưa người giàu thẳng từ hầm xe lên tầng trên, ít gặp người dân trên phố.

q5.text: Before 1850, top-floor rooms had the highest rents in the city.

steps: Đoạn 1: Tầng trên cùng rẻ và ít ai thích (cheap and unpopular).

q6.text: Otis's safety brake stopped the platform after it fell only a few inches.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...dropped only a few inches before his automatic safety brake locked it safely in place."

q7.text: The word 'penthouse' was first invented by a New York newspaper in 1854.

steps: Đoạn 3: Có nhắc từ penthouses, nhưng không nói báo New York phát minh ra từ này.

q8.text: High-speed elevators allow skyscraper residents to go directly from garages to upper suites.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...carry rich residents straight from underground car parks to top-floor apartments..."
